content: A ban on research involving great apes, or strict limitations on their use in scientific studies, is currently enforced in countries such as the Netherlands, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, Sweden, Germany, and Austria. Notably, Austria is the only country in the world that has extended this prohibition to include experiments on lesser apes, such as gibbons, as well. These nations have determined that chimpanzees, bonobos, gorillas, and orangutans possess cognitive and behavioral traits that are so closely aligned with those of humans that subjecting them to research is considered unethical. When the United Kingdom announced its ban in 1986, the British Home Secretary stated that the decision was fundamentally a matter of morality. He emphasized that the cognitive and behavioral characteristics of these animals make it unethical to treat them as disposable subjects for research purposes. Despite this ban, the United Kingdom continues to permit the use of other primates, such as macaques and marmosets, in laboratory research. In 2006, the permanence of the UK’s ban on great ape research was questioned by Colin Blakemore, the head of the Medical Research Council at the time. While Blakemore clarified that he saw no immediate need to lift the ban, he argued that under certain extreme circumstances—such as the emergence of a lethal pandemic virus that affected both humans and great apes—experiments on chimpanzees, orangutans, and even gorillas might become necessary. The British Union for the Abolition of Vivisection criticized Blakemore’s position, describing it as backward-looking.
